entry.title: Does your PhD’s pedigree decide your career more than your papers do?

link.title: Does your PhD’s pedigree decide your career more than your papers do?

entry.content:
You already suspected this. Now there’s a number for it, and the number is worse than you thought.

A 2022 study in Nature, “Quantifying hierarchy and dynamics in US faculty hiring and retention” by K. Hunter Wapman, Sam Zhang, Aaron Clauset and Daniel Larremore, mapped the doctoral training and employment of 238,676 tenure-track professors across 387 PhD-granting US universities over the decade 2011 to 2020. It’s the most complete picture of academic hiring anyone has assembled, and it says the thing nobody on a hiring committee wants said out loud: where you got your PhD predicts your career more cleanly than almost anything about the work you did there.

Eighty percent of professors come from twenty percent of schools

Start with the concentration. Just 20.4 percent of PhD-granting universities produced 80 percent of all tenure-track faculty in the country. Narrow it further and it gets starker: five universities, Michigan, Wisconsin-Madison, Berkeley, Harvard and Stanford, trained about one in eight American professors between them, 13.8 percent out of hundreds of doors. If you didn’t train at a top-fifth institution, four out of five of your future colleagues did.

The hierarchy only runs one way

The authors reconstructed a prestige ranking purely from who hires whom, then asked how often people move up it. The answer, depending on the field, is that only 5 to 23 percent of faculty end up at a university more prestigious than the one that granted their doctorate. In the humanities, upward mobility was about 12 percent. For most people the hierarchy is a one-way street: you’re hired at your level or below, almost never above. Prestige flows downhill, and it rarely climbs back.

The authors are direct about what this implies. Prestige is overvalued in hiring, and a researcher has little chance of landing somewhere more elite than where they trained. Your doctoral institution is less a starting line than a ceiling.

And it does not stop at getting hired

The same study followed who leaves, and attrition is not evenly spread. Faculty trained at more prestigious institutions stay longer, and the group with the lowest attrition of all is white male faculty from top programs. The paper also finds that recent gains in women’s representation come mostly from demographic turnover and earlier hiring changes, and that on current trends most fields will not reach gender parity without further change. The hierarchy is not only who gets in. It is also who stays.

What the study does not say

I want to be careful, because a bleak number invites overreading.

This is US, tenure-track, PhD-granting universities only. It says nothing direct about liberal-arts colleges, industry, national labs, or other countries, and careers outside that slice may look different.

“Prestige” here is defined by the hiring network itself, who places graduates where, not by an outside measure of quality. That is deliberate, and it is also circular by construction: the network draws its own hierarchy. It tells you how the system sorts people, not that the sorting tracks merit. The authors’ own reading is the opposite, that the sorting overweights pedigree.

And it is a snapshot of one decade. It measures placement, not the quality of anyone’s scholarship. Plenty of the best work in any field is done by people the hierarchy placed far from the top. The study does not dispute that. It shows that doing the work and being placed by the work are two different games.

What to do if you did not train at a top-fifth school

So what do you do with a fact you can’t change? You can’t re-run your PhD at Berkeley. That door closes the day you finish.

The answer is narrow and a little cold. If the one variable that most predicts your placement is fixed, then the variables you can still move are worth more, not less. Your output is one. Whether the right people can find that output is the other, and it is the one most people leave entirely to chance. I run a company premised on that second lever, so discount me accordingly. But the logic holds without me: in a system that hands a large advantage to a pedigree you can’t acquire, the small controllable edges are the whole game for everyone who didn’t get the pedigree.

None of this promises that being findable will vault you up the hierarchy. This paper is fairly clear that almost nothing vaults you up the hierarchy. The claim is more modest: the prestige you were assigned at 27 is doing a lot of quiet work in rooms you’ll never sit in, so the parts of your visibility you actually control are worth taking seriously. The alternative is to leave the one lever you’ve unpulled, and hope the committee reads your papers instead of your CV’s letterhead. How often do you think they do?
entry.summary: A 2022 Nature study of 238,676 professors finds 80% trained at just 20% of universities, five schools produced one in eight, and only 5 to 23% ever work somewhere more prestigious than their PhD. What that means if you didn't train at an elite school.

entry.title: What does a great mentor actually give you? (Not their topic.)

link.title: What does a great mentor actually give you? (Not their topic.)

entry.content:
Everyone gives the same advice to a new PhD student. Find a great mentor, and do what they do. The first half is right. The second half, according to a large study of how scientific careers actually unfold, is close to backwards.

The paper is Yifang Ma, Satyam Mukherjee and Brian Uzzi, “Mentorship and protégé success in STEM fields”, in PNAS (2020). They assembled genealogical records on nearly 40,000 scientists who published 1,167,518 papers in biomedicine, chemistry, math and physics between 1960 and 2017, and asked a question most of us only answer with anecdotes: does having a great mentor actually change where you end up, and if so, what is it that gets transmitted?

Their headline: mentorship is associated with a 2x to 4x higher chance that a protégé wins a major prize, gets into the National Academy of Sciences, or becomes what they call a superstar, compared with matched protégés who had similar talent and similar starting odds. Not a small nudge.

What the mentor is actually transmitting

Here is the clever part of the design. They found clusters of mentors with similar records and reputations, who attracted protégés of similar talent. Within each cluster, one mentor had something extra: they went on to win a prize. Crucially, the skill that made them prizeworthy existed before the prize was awarded, which means their protégés were exposed to it early, before anyone knew to call it special.

And the authors are specific about what that hidden skill is. In their words, it is “skill in creating and communicating prizewinning research.” Read that twice. It is not only about having good ideas. It is about creating and communicating them. The thing that separates the future laureate from an equally credentialed peer is partly the ability to make important work legible to other people, and that ability rubs off on the students standing nearby. I run a company built on the second half of that sentence, so take my enthusiasm with salt. But it is their sentence, not mine.

The counterintuitive part: do not copy your mentor

Now the finding that should change behavior. Protégés did not succeed most by working on their mentor’s topics. They succeeded by studying original topics, and by coauthoring only a small fraction of their papers with the mentor. The students who broke away and staked out their own ground did better than the ones who stayed in the mentor’s lane. Mentorship also predicted something related: protégés who pioneered their own research topics, and who were more likely to be midcareer late bloomers than instant stars.

So the transmission is real, but it is not imitation. You absorb the mentor’s tacit skill for making and communicating important work, and then you point it at a question that’s yours. Copying the topic is the mistake. Copying the craft is the point.

What the study can’t rule out

I like this paper, and I don’t want to oversell it.

It is observational. Nobody randomly assigned students to great mentors. The authors work hard with matched comparisons to rule out the boring explanation, that great mentors simply attract great students, and that matching is the backbone of the whole argument. But matching narrows a gap, it does not close it. Some of the 2x to 4x could still be selection they could not see.

The models explain 34 to 44 percent of the variance in protégé success. That is a lot for social data, and it also means most of what decides a career still sits outside the model. Mentorship matters. It is not destiny.

And it is STEM, mostly the elite tip of STEM, measured through prizes and academy membership and “superstardom.” Those are the outcomes at the top of a very steep pyramid. Whether the same pattern holds for a solid, non-prizewinning career, or in the humanities, this paper cannot say.

Why you should care, on either side of the desk

If you’re early, the practical read is unusually clean. Choose a mentor for the tacit skill you can only learn by proximity: how they frame a problem, how they decide what’s worth doing, how they make it land with other people. Then don’t spend your twenties as their coauthor. Take the craft and leave the topic.

If you’re the mentor, the uncomfortable implication is that the most valuable thing you pass on isn’t the project you hand a student, and not the papers you write together. It’s a way of working that you might not even know you’ve, including how you make your work visible. You can’t teach that by keeping students on your own topics. You teach it by letting them leave.

I keep coming back to that one word in the abstract: communicating. The study says the hidden, mentorable skill behind a celebrated career includes the ability to make the work known. If that is right, then “just do good science and it will speak for itself” is not merely incomplete advice. It is the one thing the laureates apparently did not believe. Did yours?
entry.summary: A 2020 PNAS study of nearly 40,000 scientists finds a great mentor's biggest gift is a tacit skill for creating and communicating important research, and that protégés who copy their mentor's topic do worse than those who strike out on their own.

entry.title: Who else is on your Google Scholar profile?

link.title: Who else is on your Google Scholar profile?

entry.content:
You type your own name into Google Scholar to see what a reviewer would see, and something is off. There’s a paper you never wrote, in a field next to yours, sitting under your name. And a paper you did write, the one you actually want people to find, is nowhere on the profile. Somewhere out there is a namesake, and Google Scholar has quietly mixed the two of you together.

Here is the short version. A Google Scholar profile is an attribution record, and right now that record is upstream of almost everything: who gets found, who gets cited, and who an AI assistant names when someone asks a question your work answers. If the record is wrong, the credit goes to the wrong place. Cleaning it up takes an afternoon, and this is how.

Why a messy profile is now an attribution problem

For years a stray paper on your profile was cosmetic. A slightly inflated citation count, a category that didn’t fit. Annoying, not costly.

That changed when discovery started running through machines. An AI answer engine doesn’t judge your work. It retrieves text, and it attributes that text to whoever the record says produced it. If your profile says you wrote a namesake’s paper, that’s now part of your machine-readable identity. If a real paper of yours is missing, or split across two half-records, the machine has less to connect to you, and it reaches for whoever is easier to attribute cleanly. I wrote about that pull toward the already-visible in what AI search actually sees.

So the goal is not a longer profile. It is a correct one. Every paper on it’s yours, every paper of yours is on it, and your name reads the same way each time.

Step 1: Remove the papers that aren’t yours

Sign in and open your own profile, the one you can edit. Read the list slowly, top to bottom, and flag anything you didn’t write. Namesakes cluster in adjacent fields, so a wrong paper often looks plausible at a glance.

To remove one, tick the checkbox to its left and click the Delete button in the bar at the top of the list. If you would rather work from the paper itself, open it and use the correction option to say you’re not an author. Either way it leaves your profile.

Step 2: Add back the ones that are, and merge the splits

Now the opposite problem: your own papers that never made it on, or that Scholar recorded twice.

To add a missing paper, use the add button (the plus above your article list) and choose to add articles. Search your name, then search every variant of it: initials, maiden name, transliterations, the spelling a copy editor once “fixed.” Tick the ones that are actually yours and add them. Note that Scholar will not merge two whole profiles into one. If a second, ghost profile exists, this is how you pull its articles onto your main one.

For a paper that appears twice, click the “Title” column header so the duplicates line up next to each other. Tick both, click Merge, and keep the version with the cleanest metadata. Merging also stitches split citation counts back together, which fixes a number that was always yours.

Step 3: Pick one name and keep it

Most attribution damage comes from one thing: publishing under three spellings of the same name.

Decide on one canonical form. Click the edit icon next to your name and set it. Then use that exact form from now on, on submissions, on your ORCID record, in your institutional bio. Consistency is what lets a machine collapse a career’s worth of papers into one person, which is the whole point of the exercise. (This is the same identity hygiene behind personal branding for researchers.)

Step 4: Turn on alerts, then look at yourself as a stranger

A profile doesn’t stay clean on its own, because Scholar keeps adding papers it thinks are yours, and a namesake’s next paper is a coin flip.

Two settings help. First, configure article updates so Scholar emails you to review new additions instead of adding them silently. That one change stops the intruder problem from coming back. Second, use the Follow button at the top of your profile to get email when new articles are attributed to you and when your work is cited, so you notice a wrong merge the week it happens rather than a year later.

Then do the check you started with, deliberately. Open a private browser window, or sign out, and search your name the way a grant reviewer or an AI crawler would, with no login and no memory of what should be there. If the public profile shows only your work, and shows all of it, you’re done.

Common questions

How do I remove a paper that isn’t mine? Tick its checkbox and click Delete in the top bar, or open the paper and mark that you’re not an author.

Can I merge two profiles? No. Keep one as your main profile and pull the other’s articles onto it with the add button.

Does a split citation count hurt me? Yes, quietly. Two half-records show two small numbers instead of one real one, and both humans and machines read the smaller figure.

Where this fits

Attribution is the unglamorous half of visibility, and it’s easy to skip because nothing breaks loudly when you get it wrong. Loud Camel’s scan checks it for you: it flags papers attributed to the wrong person and your own work that Scholar has dropped or split, and it drafts the outreach that a clean profile makes possible. It drafts. It never sends anything on its own, and you approve every message. Fix the record first, though, with us or without us. A machine can only credit you correctly if the record already does.
entry.summary: A practical guide to cleaning up your Google Scholar profile: remove a namesake's papers, add back your own missing or split records, and fix attribution so search and AI credit the right author.

entry.title: Should a language model review your paper?

link.title: Should a language model review your paper?

entry.content:
You submit a paper and then you wait. Weeks pass, then months. When the reviews finally land, one of them is three sentences long and the other clearly read a different paper than the one you wrote. Now turn the desk around. Your own inbox is holding four review requests, three from editors you’ve never met, and you’re the same tired person who owes everyone else a review by Friday. If either of those scenes made you wince, you already understand the problem this paper is chewing on.

The paper is a 2025 preprint, “AI and the Future of Academic Peer Review” by Sebastian Porsdam Mann and colleagues (arXiv:2509.14189). Its argument, said plainly and up front: a language model can responsibly take over narrow, supervised parts of peer review, and it must not take over the human judgment that makes a review worth reading.

The system is not lightly strained

The authors are blunt about the state of things. They describe “long publication delays, escalating reviewer burden concentrated on a small minority of scholars, inconsistent quality and low inter-reviewer agreement,” on top of the usual systematic biases. And the discouraging part: “decades of human-centered reforms have yielded only marginal improvements.” So the load really is piled on a few people, which is the second scene above, and the fixes we already tried barely moved it.

What the model is allowed to do

Here is the useful half. The paper argues that “targeted, supervised LLM assistance can plausibly improve error detection, timeliness, and reviewer workload without displacing human judgment.” Think of the mechanical jobs: checking whether a proof holds, flagging a citation that is missing, catching a statistic that cannot be right, pointing a reviewer at the three claims out of fifty that actually need a human to think hard. The authors go further and sketch fine-tuned, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent systems that could make review “more reliable, auditable, and interdisciplinary.” Keep the word supervised in view. It is carrying most of the weight in that sentence.

What the model is not allowed to do

Now the half that should worry you. The authors list the failure modes as “hallucination, confidentiality, gaming, novelty recognition, and loss of trust,” and they refuse to file these under details to patch later. In their word, these problems are “constitutive” of what makes review legitimate, which makes them “governance choices as much as technical capacity.”

Two of them are worth stopping on. Confidentiality: your unpublished manuscript is a secret you handed to one editor, and pasting it into a commercial chatbot quietly breaks that promise for everyone who trusted you with it. And novelty recognition, which is my shorthand for the model faking competence: a language model is very good at producing a confident, fluent review of a paper it doesn’t actually understand, and a genuinely new idea is close to the one thing it never saw in training. A tired human at least half-knows when they are bluffing. The model does not know at all.

My take, with the caveats a preprint earns

Where do I land? The paper’s own recommendation is the sober one, and I agree with it: reject both “uncritical adoption [and] reflexive rejection,” and run instead “carefully scoped pilots with explicit evaluation metrics, transparency, and accountability.”

Two caveats before you quote it at your next lab meeting. First, this is a preprint. It has not itself been through peer review, which is a small irony worth saying out loud, so treat its framing as a well-argued position and not a settled result. Second, “supervised” is cheap to write and expensive to enforce. The thing that goes wrong is not a rogue AI seizing the journal. It is a swamped reviewer who lets the model draft the whole review and then skims the output, and no editor can see that from the outside.

Why you should care, on both sides of the desk

If you submit papers, the confidentiality problem is already yours, today, policy or no policy: someone in your review pile may be feeding your manuscript to a model right now. If you review papers, the honest question the paper hands you is which parts of your own reviewing are the mechanical parts a machine could take, and which parts are the judgment you’re willing to sign your name under. That line is the entire debate, compressed.

The paper doesn’t draw the line for you, and I’m not going to pretend I can either. But once you’ve waited most of a year for two careless reviews, “let the machine help, carefully” stops sounding reckless and starts sounding like the least bad option on the table. I might be wrong about how careful anyone will actually bother to be.
entry.summary: A 2025 preprint by Sebastian Porsdam Mann and colleagues argues large language models should take over narrow, supervised parts of peer review, and stay away from the human judgment that makes it legitimate. My take, with a preprint's caveats.

entry.title: Does a career grant actually stop brain drain?

link.title: Does a career grant actually stop brain drain?

entry.content:
A talented postdoc from a smaller country takes a two-year contract in Boston, then a better one in Zurich, and somewhere along the way stops planning the trip home. You have probably watched this happen to someone. Countries that train researchers keep losing them to countries that pay better and cite better, and everyone from the European Commission down has spent decades trying to reverse the flow. The obvious lever is money: hand the returning scientist a grant, and maybe they stay.

Does that lever actually work? A new paper in Quantitative Science Studies is, as far as I can tell, the first study to check the question quantitatively, and the short answer is: a little, and mostly for the people you would least expect.

The paper is Marco Seeber and colleagues, “The effect of public funding on long-term relocation of experienced researchers”, published in 2025. They studied the Marie Curie Career Integration Grant, or CIG, a scheme under the European Union’s Seventh Framework Programme that was built to counter the European brain drain to third countries and to help experienced researchers settle for the long term inside an EU member or associated country. It is exactly the kind of “come back and stay” incentive that governments love to announce and rarely measure.

Here is the finding, stated the way the authors state it. Getting the grant was associated with a 9.4% higher chance of long-term relocation in the host institution, and an 8.2% higher chance in the host country. Not nothing. Not enormous.

How did they measure it? They took the applicants to three CIG calls, from 2011, 2012, and 2013, reconstructed each person’s career from Scopus records and their CVs, and then compared where the funded applicants ended up against the applicants who applied and did not get the money. So the comparison is not grantees versus the general population; it is grantees versus their own rejected peers, which is a much fairer test.

The part I find most interesting is who the grant helped. The effect was concentrated in the applicants who had the fewest other options: people without a tenured position, scientists in the soft sciences, people who were not returning to their home country, and people moving to institutions that are not highly ranked. For a well-funded scientist heading to a top lab, the grant changed little, because that person already had other money and other offers. For someone with none of that, it moved the needle. A subsidy matters most to the person who cannot easily replace it. That is almost boring to say out loud, but it is good to see it hold up in the data.

And one honest negative that the authors report: the grant showed no relationship with landing a tenured position, and none with scientific productivity. It helped people stay in place. On this evidence it did not make them more successful once they stayed.

Now the caveat, because this is where I get twitchy. This is a comparison, not an experiment. Nobody flipped a coin to decide who got funded. The people who won CIG grants won because a committee judged their proposals stronger, and stronger proposals tend to come from people who were already more likely to build a stable career wherever they landed. The authors are careful with their verbs, “related to,” “associated with,” and so should we be. A 9.4% gap between grantees and rejected applicants could be the grant, or it could be the same qualities that got them the grant in the first place. Matching and careful career reconstruction narrow that gap. They do not close it.

It is also one programme, run by one funder, over a handful of years, on one continent. Whether an Israeli or Canadian or Brazilian version of the same idea would buy the same 8% is an open question, and this paper cannot answer it.

So why should you care? If you’re an early or mid-career researcher weighing whether a reintegration grant is worth the application effort, this gives you a realistic number instead of a brochure promise. The grant nudges your odds. It doesn’t rewrite your career, and it’ll do the most for you precisely if you are the applicant with no fallback. If you care more broadly about where science concentrates, the sobering reading is that even a targeted, reasonably designed grant buys single-digit percentage points against the pull of richer, better-cited places. The gravity is strong.

I would like to see the randomized version of this, if any funder is ever brave enough to run one. Until then, single digits is what we’ve. Would you move countries for an 8% nudge, or does that just confirm you were leaning that way already?
entry.summary: A 2025 Quantitative Science Studies paper, the first to test the question, finds the Marie Curie Career Integration Grant raised long-term relocation odds by about 8 to 9%, mostly for researchers with the fewest other options.

entry.title: The narrative CV that stands out: what funders actually read

link.title: The narrative CV that stands out: what funders actually read

entry.content:
You open the funding call expecting the usual “list your publications,” and instead you get four empty text boxes. How did you contribute to knowledge? To individuals? To your community? To society? A thousand words, split however you like. A list of papers you could write in your sleep, and next to it, a story about your own contribution that you’ve never once written down.

That is a narrative CV, and funders are switching to it fast. The official templates from UKRI, the Royal Society, and your university’s research office tell you what each of the four boxes is for. Almost none of them tell you how to write something a reviewer will actually remember. This post is that second half: replace vague claims with specific evidence, one contribution at a time.

Which funders actually want a narrative CV?

The format began at the Royal Society in 2019 as the “Résumé for Researchers.” UKRI adopted its own version, the Résumé for Research and Innovation, or R4RI. In 2021 a Joint Funders Group signed a shared statement committing to the approach, and the signatories include UKRI, Wellcome, Cancer Research UK, the British Heart Foundation, Alzheimer’s Research UK, the NIHR, and the Royal Academy of Engineering. Several European funders are piloting their own.

The wording differs a little between them, but they share four modules:

  1. your contribution to the generation of knowledge,
  2. your contribution to the development of individuals and teams,
  3. your contribution to the wider research community,
  4. your contribution to broader society.

UKRI’s version adds an optional box for context: career breaks, secondments, and the like. Most calls give you around 1,000 words in total, split however you want, written in the first person.

Why is this harder than a publication list?

Because a publication list hides behind numbers. Forty papers, an h-index, three grants: the reader supplies the meaning. A narrative CV takes that crutch away. You’ve to say what you did and why it mattered, in plain words, and a reviewer can tell in one sentence whether you’re showing evidence or reciting a job description.

The usual failure is vagueness. “I have made significant contributions to my field and mentored many students.” That sentence could belong to anyone. It feels safe, which is exactly why people write it. It also says nothing, and a reviewer working through forty applications won’t remember yours.

How do you make each of the four modules land?

One rule covers all four: delete the adjective and write the evidence instead. Every time you reach for “influential” or “significant,” cut it and describe the specific thing that earned the word.

Knowledge. Don’t write “I published widely in leading journals.” Write what changed because of your work. “I developed a calibration method that three other labs now use to measure X” tells a reviewer more than any impact factor. Name the idea, and name who picked it up.

Development of individuals. Don’t write “I have supervised many students.” Write “I supervised a PhD student who arrived with no coding background and who now leads data engineering at [type of organisation].” One person described in real detail beats a headcount. Show the before and the after.

Wider community. Don’t write “I am active in my research community.” Write the specific act and its size. “I review for four journals, and I rebuilt our department seminar from two talks a term into a fortnightly series that now brings in external speakers.” Verbs and numbers.

Broader society. This is the box people pad the most. Don’t write “my research has real-world impact.” Write who outside academia used it, and how. “I wrote the plain-language guidance a patient charity now sends to newly diagnosed families.” If nobody outside academia has used your work yet, say plainly what you did to try. Reviewers can smell an inflated impact claim from across the room.

Notice the shape of every “do” example: a specific action, a named beneficiary or a real number, and a consequence. That is the whole trick, repeated four times.

What if your evidence is genuinely thin?

Then be honest, and be small and specific. One real, concrete example of mentoring a single person well reads as more credible than a paragraph of confident abstraction. You control how the word count is split, so put the words where your evidence is strongest and keep the thin module short. Nobody is strong in all four, and reviewers know that.

And write in the first person, in active language: led, built, taught, changed. UKRI’s own guidance asks for exactly this. Flat committee-speak is the second most common way these CVs go dead, right behind vagueness.

I’ve not sat on a UKRI panel, and reviewers differ. But every piece of funder guidance I read while writing this points the same way. Specific and honest beats grand and vague.

Where does Loud Camel fit?

Half of “contribution to knowledge” is other people using your work, and you can only describe that if you know it happened. Loud Camel tracks where your research gets cited, mentioned, and recommended, including inside AI answer engines, so that when you sit down to write module one you’re working from a real list of uptake instead of a guess. It drafts that evidence and hands it to you. It never posts or sends anything on its own. You still write the CV. You just write it from facts.

Common questions

Which funders require a narrative CV? UKRI (as the R4RI), the Royal Society, Wellcome, Cancer Research UK, the British Heart Foundation, Alzheimer’s Research UK, the NIHR, and the Royal Academy of Engineering have all committed to the narrative CV approach, with more funders piloting it. Always check the specific call, because wording and word limits vary.

How long should a narrative CV be? Most funders allow around 1,000 words across the four modules, written in the first person, and let you decide how to split the total.

What is the single most common mistake? Vagueness. Claims like “significant contributions” and “widely published” say nothing on their own. Replace every such phrase with a specific action, a named beneficiary or a number, and what changed.
entry.summary: More funders now ask for a narrative CV instead of a publication list. The official guidance tells you the four boxes to fill. Here is how to make each one land with specific evidence.

entry.title: Why do some papers keep getting cited, and most don’t?

link.title: Why do some papers keep getting cited, and most don’t?

entry.content:
Years ago, at Automattic, I looked at what made a blog post collect likes. The strongest predictor I found wasn’t the topic, the length, or the time of day. It was whether the same author’s earlier posts had collected likes. Likes bred likes. If you already had them, you got more. If you didn’t, you mostly didn’t.

Sociologists have a name for this: the Matthew effect. The rich get richer. In citation studies it goes by “preferential attachment” or “cumulative advantage,” and it is the standard answer to a question every researcher asks: why do a handful of papers get cited thousands of times while most sink without a trace?

A recent preprint says that answer is incomplete. In “Community-centric modeling of citation dynamics explains collective citation patterns in science, law, and patents” (arXiv, January 2025), Sadamori Kojaku and colleagues argue that whether a paper keeps getting cited is not mainly about the paper. It is about the community the paper sits in, and where that community’s attention happens to drift. Success, in their framing, is less about you and more about the crowd you run with.

What rich-get-richer can’t explain

Pure cumulative advantage has an awkward blind spot. If citations only flow to papers that already have citations, then a paper ignored at birth should stay ignored forever. But that is not what happens. Some papers sit unread for years, sometimes decades, and then suddenly surge. The literature calls them sleeping beauties, and the delay is called delayed recognition. The authors note that models of individual citation trajectories fail to reproduce this. You cannot get a sleeping beauty out of a machine whose only rule is “the popular get more popular.”

The idea: citations are collective decisions

Their move is to stop modelling a paper as a lone object with intrinsic pull, and start modelling the citing side. A citation, in this view, is a decision made by the authors who are writing now, and those authors cluster into communities in a high-dimensional “knowledge space.” Communities drift through that space over time. As a community moves, the work near its current location gets cited, and work it has moved away from goes quiet. That drift produces recency even though the model is never told about time. There is no explicit aging term. Papers age because attention wanders off.

It also explains sleeping beauties in a way rich-get-richer cannot. A paper published in a sparse, out-of-the-way corner of knowledge space waits. Years later a community wanders into that corner, and the old paper wakes up. The model reproduces this across all three corpora it was tested on: science, law, and patents, using a newly available U.S. case-law dataset for the legal side. The three domains share the same heavy-tailed patterns, which is part of why the authors think they are onto a general mechanism rather than a quirk of academia.

The model keeps three ingredients working together, as the authors describe them: relevance, which is how close a paper sits to where a community’s attention is; cumulative advantage, the old rich-get-richer pull, still present, just no longer alone; and fitness, something like intrinsic quality. Preferential attachment is not wrong here. It is one of three, not the whole story.

What this does not tell you

Two cautions before anyone gets excited. First, this is a preprint. It hasn’t been through peer review as I write this, and preprints get revised, sometimes heavily. Read it as a strong hypothesis, not a settled result. Second, and more important, it is a model. It reproduces collective, aggregate patterns: the shape of the distribution, the abundance of sleeping beauties across a whole field. It says almost nothing about your specific paper. Knowing that attention drifts through communities doesn’t tell you when, or whether, a community will drift toward your particular corner. A model that explains the crowd is not a plan for the individual.

Does it tell you anything useful?

Carefully, maybe one thing. If citations track where communities are looking, then being legible to the community you actually belong to isn’t vanity. It’s how you get seen at all. That is not the same as saying “promote harder and you’ll get cited.” The paper makes no such claim, and I won’t put it in the authors’ mouths. It’s closer to a reframing: a paper nobody in your community can find, or place, is a paper sitting in an empty corner of the space, waiting for a drift that may never come.

I find the collective framing convincing, and I might be wrong about that. If the mechanism is real, the uncomfortable implication is that a lot of what we call a paper’s quality is really a statement about its neighbourhood. Would your best-cited work have done as well one community over? I genuinely don’t know. Neither, quite, does the model.
entry.summary: A January 2025 preprint argues papers keep getting cited less because of intrinsic quality and more because of where their research community's attention drifts, explaining sleeping beauties that rich-get-richer models cannot.

entry.title: A reviewer looks you up before they score you. What do they find?

link.title: A reviewer looks you up before they score you. What do they find?

entry.content:
You spent months on the proposal. At some point during review, a panelist will stop reading it, open a new tab, and type your name into Google or ChatGPT. Whatever comes back sits next to your PDF while they score you. You cannot touch it on the day. You can fix most of it now.

TL;DR: Most grant and fellowship review isn’t anonymous, so the panel forms a second impression of you, outside your proposal, from whatever a quick search returns. That impression is auditable. Run the searches a reviewer would run, and check that your best work surfaces, that your name resolves to you and not a namesake, and that your own pages aren’t blocking the AI tools reviewers now use. Close the gaps before you submit, not after.

Why does what a reviewer Googles matter more than your formatting?

Almost all grant advice optimizes the document. Almost none of it optimizes what a reviewer sees when they look away from the document.

Some journal peer review hides the author’s identity, but grant and fellowship review almost never does. At NIH, NSF, the ERC, and most fellowship panels, the reviewer knows exactly whose name is on the application. Fellowships are worse in this respect, because the scheme is funding a person, not just a project, so the person is the point. Curiosity is cheap and normal. They read your career narrative, they wonder who you’re, and looking you up costs one tab.

What they find becomes a quiet input to the score. Not a line on the form. Just an impression, formed in a minute, that colors how they read the rest. A clean, current, on-topic footprint reads as low risk. A dead LinkedIn from 2016, a Scholar page that blends your work with three strangers, and nothing online about the specific topic of the proposal reads as something else. None of that’s in your PDF, and all of it’s auditable.

What should you check before you submit?

Sit down a few weeks before the deadline and run the check yourself. It takes about twenty minutes and needs nothing but a browser. Do it logged out or in a private window, so you see what a stranger sees and not what Google has personalized for you.

Does your best work surface for the query a reviewer would type?

Don’t search your own name and stop there. Search the way a panelist would: your name plus your topic, then the topic on its own. “Jane Okafor microplastics,” then “microplastics freshwater uptake.” Does your most relevant paper show up on the first screen, in Google and in an AI tool like ChatGPT or Perplexity? If your strongest work is invisible for the exact query your proposal is about, the reviewer’s search quietly contradicts your claim to own the topic.

Does your name resolve to you, not to a namesake?

Now type your name alone. If the first page belongs to a more famous cardiologist who shares it, or to a LinkedIn that’s not yours, the reviewer may never reach you at all. You can’t evict the namesake, but you can outrank them on your own turf: a personal page you control, an institutional profile that’s actually updated, an ORCID that points at your record.

Is your Google Scholar profile disambiguated and current?

Scholar auto-merges papers by matching names, so profiles routinely absorb work from strangers and drop your own. Open yours. Remove the papers that aren’t yours, add the ones it missed, and make your affiliation and listed interests current. A reviewer who lands on a profile crediting you with a physicist’s papers reads carelessness, whether or not that’s fair to you.

Does your page block the AI a reviewer is now asking?

This one is invisible and common. When a reviewer asks ChatGPT or Perplexity about you, those tools can only quote pages their crawlers are allowed to read. Many university sites and personal setups block AI crawlers by default in robots.txt: GPTBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended. OpenAI is explicit that pages opted out of its OAI-SearchBot will not appear in ChatGPT’s search answers. So your bio and publications list can be perfectly accurate and still be missing from the exact answer the panel is reading. Check your site’s robots.txt (it lives at yoursite.com/robots.txt). If your own pages are walled off, unwall the ones you want cited.

The impression is fixable, which is the whole point

Notice what these four checks have in common. None of them asks you to become a better scientist by the deadline. Each one asks whether the version of you that a stranger assembles in a minute or two matches the version in your proposal. When it doesn’t, the mismatch does the damage, and you can usually close it in an afternoon.

There is a seasonal reason to do it now. The fall grant and fellowship deadlines are a few weeks out, which means the panels that will read those proposals are a few weeks after that. The search a reviewer will run in October is the same one you can run today.

Where Loud Camel fits

This is the check Loud Camel runs for you on a schedule, so you’re not doing it by hand the week a proposal is due. It watches what surfaces for your name, whether AI tools attribute your work to you or to a stranger, and where your footprint contradicts your CV. Then it drafts the fixes and any outreach for you to approve. It drafts. It does not send anything on its own. You stay the one who decides what goes out.

None of this rescues a weak proposal. It stops a strong one from being read next to a stale page or a stranger who happens to share your name.
entry.summary: Grant and fellowship reviewers look you up mid-review. Run this pre-submission visibility check: does your best work surface for their query, is your Scholar profile disambiguated, and does your own page block the AI they ask?

entry.title: A prompt pack for academic visibility

link.title: A prompt pack for academic visibility

entry.content:
Every draft a prompt hands you goes out under your name. The reviewer sees your name on the abstract, the public venue sees your name on the answer, the conference program prints your name next to the talk. So review every output to the last letter before you send or publish it. A good name is worth more than the time the prompt saved you. Ecclesiastes 7:1 puts it as “a good name is better than fine oil,” and Nassim Taleb calls the same idea skin in the game. The prompt has none. You have all of it.

That is the whole posture for this post. What follows is a swipe file: four prompts you can paste, fill in, and run. Each comes with a “when to use” line and a one-line caveat. Several other prompts in this field guide (the plain-language summary, the outreach email, the reconnection email, the bio, the AI-search audit) live in their own posts in this series. This post collects the remaining four.

The reviewer-readable abstract prompt

When to use: you suspect a grant reviewer outside your sub-sub-field couldn’t, in 30 seconds, place where your contribution sits. This keeps technical precision but optimizes for fast field-placement.

You are a grant-panel reviewer who is a respected researcher in a field adjacent to, but not the same as, the field of the abstract you are about to receive.

Rewrite the abstract so that *you* could understand it in 30 seconds. You may keep technical terms that are well-known one field over. You must define or replace any term that is only known inside the sub-sub-field.

Structure:
1. One sentence on the question, phrased to connect to a broader body of work the reviewer would know.
2. One sentence on the method, named by its broader family (e.g. "a regression-discontinuity design", "a transformer-based encoder", "a randomized double-blind trial") rather than its sub-sub-field name.
3. Two to three sentences on the result, including the single most important number.
4. One sentence on the implication for the broader field, not just for the sub-sub-field.

Total length: 150-200 words. No marketing language. No "novel", "innovative", or "groundbreaking".

Abstract:
<PASTE ABSTRACT HERE>

Caveat: if the rewrite feels like it loses precision, that is the point. Reviewer-readable is not specialist-readable. Both versions should exist; this one goes in the grant proposal and the executive summary.

The discussion-post prompt

When to use: you found a recurring question on a public venue (StackExchange, a subreddit, a mailing list) and want a thoughtful, non-spammy answer that links back to your work.

You are a thoughtful, slightly cynical researcher who hates self-promotional content but loves explaining things clearly.

I will give you (a) a public question, (b) the abstract or summary of my paper, and (c) which sub-question of the public question my paper answers.

Draft a response that:
- Opens by answering the public question directly. Do NOT mention my paper in the first paragraph.
- In paragraphs 2-3, gives the substantive answer using plain language. Use a number if there is a number. Cite 1-2 well-known references that are not mine.
- In the final paragraph, says: "Full disclosure, I'm one of the people who worked on this. Here is our paper, which goes into <SUB-QUESTION>: <LINK>". Then mentions one open question my paper does NOT answer, to demonstrate honesty.

Total length: 250-400 words. No marketing language. No "we're excited to share". No "groundbreaking".

(a) Public question: <PASTE>
(b) My paper summary: <PASTE PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY>
(c) Sub-question my paper answers: <PASTE>

Caveat: these posts are findable for years. Make sure the answer helps even if the reader never clicks the link. The link is the cherry, not the cake.

The conference-talk-recycling prompt

When to use: you’ve a 30-minute talk and an invitation to give it to a different audience. Adapt without rewriting.

You are helping me adapt a talk I already give well to a new audience.

I will give you:
(a) the abstract of my talk as it currently is,
(b) the new audience: their field, their seniority, what they already know, what they don't.

For the new audience, propose:
1. A revised one-paragraph abstract (~120 words) optimized for THIS audience.
2. Three slides that should be ADDED at the start to bridge from what they know to what my talk assumes.
3. One slide that should be REMOVED because it assumes background this audience lacks.
4. One sentence I should add to the closing slide that connects my work to a question THIS audience cares about.

Do NOT propose rewriting the whole talk. Reuse is the point.

(a) Current talk abstract: <PASTE>
(b) New audience: <DESCRIBE>

Caveat: the model is good at proposing bridge slides and mediocre at choosing the slide to cut. Trust yourself on the cut.

The graphical-abstract prompts (peer + public)

When to use: you’ve a plain-language summary and want a visual companion in two versions. The LLM produces a layout brief, not the image; you render it in Figma, BioRender, Canva, or an image tool. Prompt A is for a peer audience and takes your abstract. Prompt B is for the general public and takes your plain-language summary.

Prompt A, peer audience:

You are a science illustrator preparing a graphical abstract for an academic audience. I will give you the abstract of a peer-reviewed paper.

Produce a layout brief (not an image) that a designer can render. Specify:
1. The layout structure, in 3-5 sentences: how many panels, how they are arranged, what flows where.
2. The text inside each box, 10 words or less per box.
3. The single key visual anchor: the one image or diagram that carries the result.
4. One bold number to feature.
5. One sentence on how this work extends prior work in the field.

Constraints:
- Must be readable at thumbnail size.
- Technical terms are fine for this audience.
- No marketing words. No "novel", "innovative", "groundbreaking".

Abstract:
<PASTE ABSTRACT HERE>

Prompt B, general public:

You are a science illustrator preparing a graphical abstract for a general audience. I will give you a plain-language summary of a research paper.

Produce a layout brief (not an image) that a designer can render. Specify:
1. A sequential narrative layout an outsider can follow in 10 seconds: the order of panels, left to right or top to bottom.
2. A plain-language caption for each panel.
3. One striking hook for the first panel.
4. One bold takeaway for the final panel.
5. A note on color, mood, and any analogy or metaphor that makes the idea land.

Constraints:
- No jargon.
- No academic-paper aesthetics.
- The first thing the viewer sees must answer "why does this matter to me?".

Plain-language summary:
<PASTE PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY HERE>

Caveat: the LLM gives a layout brief, not the image. Render it yourself and run a thumbnail-readability test before publishing.

Read it before you sign it

Same caveat that opened this post, now as a pointer: never sign your name to a draft you’ve not read to the last letter. The prompt is a draft generator, not a sender. It produces the structure; you do the part that has your name on it.

This post is part of the Loud Camel field guide to academic visibility. You can read the whole guide as a single PDF: the handbook.
entry.summary: Four reusable ChatGPT prompts for academic visibility work: a reviewer-readable abstract, a non-spammy discussion-post answer, a talk you adapt instead of rewrite, and graphical-abstract layout briefs. Verbatim, swipe-and-paste, with one caveat each.

entry.title: Does crossing fields make your paper more disruptive, or just harder?

link.title: Does crossing fields make your paper more disruptive, or just harder?

entry.content:
“Be more interdisciplinary.” Every funding call, every keynote, every senior colleague who has run out of specific advice tells you the same thing. Reach across fields. Borrow from the neighbors. It’s the safest thing you can say to a young researcher, because nobody will ever call it wrong. Safe advice and useful advice aren’t the same thing, though, and I’ve always wanted to know whether crossing fields actually makes your work land harder, or just makes it harder to do.

A 2025 paper by Alex J. Yang in the Journal of Information Science (doi.org/10.1177/01655515251330614) gives a straight answer, at least on average. Looking at 38 million papers across all fields from 1960 to 2020, Yang finds a clear positive link between how interdisciplinary a paper is and its “disruptive potential.” Papers that pull ideas from further apart tend to reshape their area more, not less. And the link has been getting stronger over time, more so in STEM than in the social sciences and humanities.

What the two words actually measure

Two words are doing a lot of work here, so it is worth being precise. Interdisciplinarity is an ex-ante input: what you drew on, read off from how varied your references are. Disruption is a post hoc score: whether later work cites your paper instead of the things it built on (you eclipsed your predecessors) or alongside them (you extended them). One is fixed the day you publish. The other only makes sense years later, once the citations arrive.

The slogan gets complicated

Now the part that undercuts the slogan. Over the same 60 years, interdisciplinarity went up and disruption went down. And bigger teams, which produce more interdisciplinary work, are less likely to be disruptive. So “be interdisciplinary” and “be disruptive” have been drifting in opposite directions across science as a whole, even while, paper by paper, the two move together. Yang also reports that the interdisciplinarity-to-disruption coupling is stronger inside larger teams, which does not obviously square with larger teams being less disruptive overall. I’m reading this from the abstract, so I would check the full text before leaning on that one.

To explain how interdisciplinarity feeds disruption, Yang points at a few candidates: how diverse the team is, how varied the references are, and delayed citation recognition. Those are the plausible machinery behind the correlation. They’re also, notice, three more things measured from the same paper trail, which is worth keeping in mind before you treat any of them as a recipe.

Where I get uneasy

Both quantities are built from citation data, and citation data flatters some things and hides others. “Interdisciplinary,” here, mostly means you cited far-apart fields. Stapling a neuroscience reference onto an economics paper counts, whether or not you did anything real with it. The disruption index is a clever proxy for “this changed the conversation,” but it’s a proxy: it’s sensitive to how many references you’ve, to a field’s citing habits, and to which database you trust. And “delayed citation recognition,” one of the mechanisms Yang points to, is a polite way of saying interdisciplinary work often sits ignored for years before it disrupts anything, if it ever does. The average is positive. The variance around that average is the part that lands on you personally.

What to do if you are the one deciding

So what does a researcher deciding how far to reach do with this? Not much, if you read it as “reach further, score higher.” A 38-million-paper average is a fact about the population, not a promise about your next paper, and the team-size paradox says the lever isn’t simply adding collaborators and citations from more fields. The honest reading is narrower. When a problem genuinely needs a second field, the evidence says crossing over tends to pay off in impact, and pays off more now than it used to. When the problem does not need it, importing a distant reference to look interdisciplinary is just noise that a citation counter happens to reward. And the payoff is not evenly spread: the effect is stronger in STEM than in the social sciences and humanities, so the same reach across fields is not worth the same everywhere. If you work outside the hard sciences, the average that this paper reports is quieter than the headline sounds.

I like this paper because it refuses the easy version of its own headline. Interdisciplinarity is linked to disruption, yes. Disruption is also falling while interdisciplinarity rises. And bigger teams do more of one and less of the other. That is messier than “cross fields, win bigger,” and messier is usually closer to true. Whether your particular bridge between two fields disrupts anything, the index will only tell you in a decade. Would you make the same bet if the payoff were that slow, and that uncertain?
entry.summary: A 2025 Journal of Information Science study of 38 million papers finds interdisciplinary work links to higher disruptive potential on average, even as disruption fell while interdisciplinarity rose, with an uneven payoff across fields.
